issues.title: Client certificates / CertificateRequest (Section 3.1)
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
### CertificateRequest optional (Section 3.1)

Backlog note: may be removed along with client cert caching.

- [ ] **Question:** Server MAY send empty extension in CR — do clients need it to send CT extension?
- [ ] **Current understanding:** Yes per draft (client MUST NOT send CT extension unless server sent CR extension)
- [ ] **Action:** Verify and document

**Context (EKR):** The client/server setting is not symmetrical: the server often does not know the client identity in advance, so caching semantics for client certificates need explicit treatment (see discussion in this issue history).

---
**This issue is the source of truth** for this topic. **POC working copy:** [`docs/draft-backlog.md`](https://github.com/yaronf/pqc-continuity-poc/blob/main/docs/draft-backlog.md) in pqc-continuity-poc — update that file when this issue changes.

issues.title: Introduction: security threat + cite EKR (informative reference)
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
### Introduction (draft) — motivation for readers

**Security threat.** A cryptanalytic break or emergency affecting classical signature schemes can leave previously issued TLS (and PKI) credentials vulnerable to a capable adversary. Deployments may need to migrate authentication to post-quantum algorithms quickly and to **avoid downgrade** to broken classical algorithms for peers that have already accepted a **commitment** to PQC. That “emergency migration” framing—why rollback is dangerous once clients have cached a restriction—is a core motivation for PQC Continuity.

**Informative reference:** Eric Rescorla’s [Educated Guesswork — PQ emergency](https://educatedguesswork.org/posts/pq-emergency/) gives an accessible, informal description of this threat and response pattern.

### Draft action

- [ ] Add citation in draft (Introduction or informative references).

---
**This issue is the source of truth** for this topic. **POC working copy:** [`docs/draft-backlog.md`](https://github.com/yaronf/pqc-continuity-poc/blob/main/docs/draft-backlog.md) in pqc-continuity-poc — update that file when this issue changes.

issues.title: Certificate chains: mixed chains; align draft with strict POC policy
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
### Draft gaps (POC tests A3, A5)

| Test | Scenario | Implied gap |
|------|----------|-------------|
| A3 | PQC leaf + RSA intermediate (mixed chain) | Draft does not specify behavior for mixed chains |
| A5 | Mixed chain (PQC leaf + traditional CA) | Draft does not specify behavior for mixed chains |

- [ ] **A3, A5:** Add normative text on mixed chains (PQC leaf + traditional CA/intermediate).

### Clarifications (Section 3.1)

- [ ] **Question:** PQC leaf + traditional intermediate — does draft imply leaf-only PQC?
  - **POC policy (implemented):** If any certificate in the full verified chain (EE, intermediates, root) is non-PQC, abort the handshake. A non-PQC intermediate or root breaks quantum-resistance and could indicate a CRQC attack on a CA.
  - **Open:** Should the draft mandate this explicitly? The current text only says the EE cert must be PQC; it is silent on intermediates and roots.

### Proposal

When PQC Continuity applies, the draft should be **strict**: mixed chains (e.g. PQC EE with a non-PQC issuer chain, or any non-PQC cert in the validated chain) **MUST** be rejected with a specified alert—aligned with the POC—rather than staying silent.

**Related:** Mention in prose that for PQ resistance the entire chain should be PQ-signed even if the draft cannot always mandate it in all deployments.

---
**This issue is the source of truth** for this topic. **POC working copy:** [`docs/draft-backlog.md`](https://github.com/yaronf/pqc-continuity-poc/blob/main/docs/draft-backlog.md) in pqc-continuity-poc — update that file when this issue changes.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
**Current POC behavior** ([pqc-continuity-poc](https://github.com/yaronf/pqc-continuity-poc)): after path validation, if **any** certificate in the verified chain (EE, intermediates, trust anchor) is not treated as PQC, the implementation **aborts the handshake**. Rationale: a traditional intermediate or root breaks end-to-end post-quantum resistance for the commitment and may indicate a mis-issued or attacked chain.

**Proposal for the draft:** When PQC Continuity applies (peer has sent / is bound by the CT extension and caching rules), the document should be **strict**: **mixed chains** (e.g. PQC EE with a non-PQC issuer chain, or any non-PQC cert in the validated chain) MUST be rejected with a specified alert—aligned with this POC policy—rather than staying silent or informational only. This closes the A3/A5 gaps relative to the POC test plan (mixed-chain scenarios).

issues.title: CDNs and middleboxes
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
### CDNs and middleboxes (draft section)

- [ ] Add draft text on **CDN provisioning** (different chains for the same origin), **middlebox** behavior, and how commitments relate to **origin identity** rather than a specific presented chain.

**Notes (from earlier issue text):** CDNs are provisioned by the origin; different CDNs may present different chains for the same server. Middleboxes that must not break traffic should not commit spuriously; breakage can occur if a middlebox is a PQC client but not a PQC server while the origin has already committed. Commitments are keyed per origin (e.g. DNS name), not the entire chain, because an attacker may replace the chain.

---
**This issue is the source of truth** for this topic. **POC working copy:** [`docs/draft-backlog.md`](https://github.com/yaronf/pqc-continuity-poc/blob/main/docs/draft-backlog.md) in pqc-continuity-poc — update that file when this issue changes.

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body: The most important point is that recovery is super-easy - just get a PQC cert for the server and install it. This would recover everybody other than clients that are behind a misbehaving middlebox.

issues.title: Appendix: design alternatives (trust anchors, HSTS, etc.)
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
### Appendix: Design alternatives (draft)

- [ ] Optional draft **appendix**: compare PQC Continuity to other approaches (e.g. trust anchors in DNS, HSTS-style patterns, layering tradeoffs).

**Ideas to cover (informative):**

- **Trust anchors:** DNS often owned separately from server operators; trust-anchor records do not pin a single algorithm family; clients may still accept certs under unpublished local anchors (rollback remains possible).
- **HSTS:** HTTP-specific; pinning/middlebox breakage concerns; app layer may need exact PQ algorithm lists; origin takeover can “brick” similarly; cache-poisoning classes differ (e.g. client-side attacks).

Use this issue for scratch notes; final text belongs in the draft appendix.

issues.title: Wire format: drop `signature_algorithm` from CT extension
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
### Drop `signature_algorithm` from CT extension

- [ ] **Proposal:** Remove `signature_algorithm` (2 bytes) from the Certificate extension body, leaving only `algorithm_validity_period` (4 bytes). Full analysis: [pqc-continuity-poc `docs/analysis-drop-algorithm-field.md`](https://github.com/yaronf/pqc-continuity-poc/blob/main/docs/analysis-drop-algorithm-field.md).

- [ ] **Rationale:** Per-algorithm pinning is not enforceable against an active attacker — the attacker can steer TLS negotiation to any algorithm the client advertises, regardless of the cached value. The integrity check (A1/A2/P5) is real but narrow: it detects a misbehaving server, not the CRQC attacker the draft is designed against. The registry is still required for the "is cert PQC?" gating check; dropping the field removes scheme-matching from the parse path but not the PQC-cert check itself.

- [ ] **Impact if adopted:** Extension shrinks from 6 to 4 bytes. A1/A2/P5 error categories disappear. PQC→PQC server migration is free (no cache update needed). Mixed-chain and empty-body semantics are unaffected.

- [ ] **Action:** Propose in draft; if accepted, update POC implementation (`poc-backlog.md`).

---
**This issue is the source of truth** for this topic. **POC working copy:** [`docs/draft-backlog.md`](https://github.com/yaronf/pqc-continuity-poc/blob/main/docs/draft-backlog.md) in pqc-continuity-poc — update that file when this issue changes.

| P4 | Malformed extension data (wrong length) | Draft does not specify: reject handshake or ignore? |

issues.title: Normative validation: P5, EE `signature_algorithm` mismatch, CT placement
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
### Draft gap — POC test P5

| Test | Scenario | Implied gap |
|------|----------|-------------|
| P5 | Unknown SignatureScheme in extension | Draft says recipient must validate; does not say abort — POC aborts with `illegal_parameter` |

- [ ] **P5:** Add explicit requirement to **reject** unknown/invalid `SignatureScheme` (e.g. `illegal_parameter`).

### Signature algorithm mismatch (Section 3.1)

- [ ] **Question:** `signature_algorithm` does not match cert — MUST NOT cache or reject handshake?
  - Current draft (§3.3) implies validation failure → don't cache, but does not mandate abort.
  - **POC:** Extension scheme must exactly match the EE cert public key; wrong PQC alg, legacy alg, or unknown scheme → **`illegal_parameter`** (RFC 8446 §6.2).
  - **Action:** Draft **MUST** abort with `illegal_parameter` if `signature_algorithm` does not match the EE cert's public key.

### CT extension placement (Section 3.1)

- [ ] If the CT extension appears on any `CertificateEntry` other than the first (EE), recipients **MUST** abort with **`illegal_parameter`**.

---

issues.title: `algorithm_validity_period == 0`: semantics + operational stale-cache risk
issues.author: yaronf
issues.body:
### Zero period semantics (Section 3.1, 3.3)

- [ ] **Question:** Sender with `algorithm_validity_period == 0`: commitment or opt-out?
- [ ] **Action:** Clarify; test both interpretations

### Zero validity: operational risk (Section 3.3)

- [ ] **Gap:** Operators switching to **0** after advertising positive validity: clients that already cached may stay PQC-only until prior expiry (months/years). Validity **0** is not instant global revocation.
- [ ] **Action:** Operational considerations: operators must wait at least `max(previously_advertised_validity)` before assuming all clients cleared cache.

---

comments.author: yaronf
comments.body:
Scope update (post GitHub #9): the Certificate extension no longer carries a `SignatureScheme`; PQC vs traditional is determined only from the EE certificate.

For this issue, treat **PQC** as one bucket: **pure-PQ** EE certs and **composite-PQ** EE certs (per {{?I-D.ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs}}—composite is a **single** signature algorithm at the protocol/PKIX layer, not per-component policy mapping). The draft should cite that draft for composite and avoid implying fine-grained mapping of certificate components to separate TLS schemes.

Normative work here is clarifying that single coarse classification for enforcement, not IANA/wire `SignatureScheme` in the extension.

issues.title: Section 3.4: is "the port" the authority port or the connected port?
issues.author: Salehin-Sammo
issues.body:
Section 3.4 (L307-310) says the cache key must include "the port":

The client MUST key each cache entry by the authenticated TLS server identity from [RFC9525], the port, and whether the handshake is connection-oriented (TLS) or datagram (DTLS).

The text does not say which port this is. It could be the authority port from the URI. It could be the TCP port the client actually connected to. Most of the time these are the same, so the question never comes up.

They differ when an HTTPS RR carries a port SvcParam. The connection then goes to the port given in the SvcParam, while the origin and the RFC 9525 reference identity keep the authority port (RFC 9460 Section 9.1). The two readings then give opposite answers about whether a cached commitment applies to that connection.

This matters beyond tidiness. Under the connected-port reading, someone who can forge or influence an HTTPS RR can move a client to a different port of the same identity without changing the origin. The commitment lookup then misses. Under the authority-port reading the lookup hits and that path closes. I am filing a separate issue shortly about the scope of the cache key, and which of these two readings you intend decides whether that issue is reachable at all.

If the authority port is what you intend, here is suggested text:

... the authority port of the URI (which may differ from the transport port when an HTTPS RR supplies a port SvcParam) ...

I am happy to send a pull request if that is the reading you want.

Filed by Nazmus Salehin Sammo, Melbourne Institute of Technology, Melbourne, Australia. Student ID MIT252100. Contact: MIT252100@stud.mit.edu.au

issues.title: Section 3.6 rule 2: is cache clearing on receipt, or on handshake completion?
issues.author: Salehin-Sammo
issues.body:
This is a question about Section 3.6 rule 2, with a short fix if the answer is what I think it is. I want to open with your own implementation, because it already answers this question and the draft does not.

Your implementation already does the right thing
In the reference implementation, both the cache update and the cache delete are deferred to SSL_CB_HANDSHAKE_DONE, and are flushed only if SSL_get_verify_result() == X509_V_OK. The source comment explains exactly why:

The CT parse_cb fires during tls_process_server_certificate(), before ssl_verify_cert_chain() runs. We must not write the cache until we know the peer's certificate chain is trusted.

That is right. My concern is that none of it appears in the normative text. A second implementer who reads Section 3.6 rule 2 literally would be conformant, and would not do this.

The asymmetry in the text
Rule 1's caching bullet (L351-352) carries a timing condition:

Otherwise, the client SHOULD cache the commitment after the handshake completes successfully.

Rule 2 fires on receipt (L361-362):

If the client holds unexpired cached information for the server, and receives the extension from the server:
and its first bullet (L364-365) has no timing condition at all:

If the algorithm_validity_period is zero, the client MUST clear the cached information for this server.
In TLS 1.3 the Certificate message is necessarily parsed before the signature that authenticates it exists on the wire (RFC 8446 Section 4.4). So on a literal reading, the clear happens before CertificateVerify and before path validation. The handshake then fails, but the stored state is already gone.

Why I think the text allows both readings
Section 4 (L421-426) says clients enforce "until they observe zero on a completed handshake". That points to the safe reading, but Section 4 is Operational Considerations and is not normative.
Section 3.4's "authenticated TLS server identity" reads as a rule about how the key is composed, not as a timing condition. Section 4.1 says this directly: entries are keyed by authenticated server identity, "not by a particular chain".
Rule 3 (L374-376) already defends the strip version of this case. It says a client which "receives no extension ... SHOULD NOT modify its cache". So adversarial content on the clearing path was clearly considered. Injection of a zero value is the other half of that case, and it is not guarded.
The draft requires three other actions on this same message before authentication (Section 3.2, and Section 3.3 twice). All three of those fail closed. The clear is the only one that fails open, and the text does not separate the two kinds.
RFC 8446 does not supply an ordering rule here. Section 4.4.2.4 imposes none.
Precedent in the model the draft names
HSTS, which Section 1 and Section 3.7 name as the model, puts this gate in the processing rule rather than in the storage-key rule. RFC 6797 Section 8.1 requires a clean secure transport before any state change, and Section 14.3 gives a forged max-age=0 as the reason for that gate. RFC 7469 Section 2.3.1 does the same for pin deletion.

I am not claiming a new attack. This condition has been in HSTS since 2012, and the draft says it is modelled on HSTS. My only observation is that the condition did not carry across into the normative text here.

The question
Section 3.6 rule 2 fires when the client "receives the extension from the server", and its first bullet is a MUST to clear the cached commitment. Rule 1's caching bullet says "after the handshake completes successfully". Rule 2's clearing bullet says nothing. Is the clear meant to happen on receipt of the Certificate message, that is, before CertificateVerify and before path validation? Or only after the handshake completes?

Suggested fix
If the algorithm_validity_period is zero, the client MUST clear the cached information for this server after the handshake completes successfully.
This lines rule 2 up with rule 1, with the existing non-normative wording in Section 4, and with what the reference implementation already does.

One piece of supporting data
I looked at where seven TLS stacks parse and dispatch per-CertificateEntry extensions relative to chain validation. The stacks were OpenSSL, BoringSSL, NSS, rustls, Go, GnuTLS and wolfSSL. In all seven, dispatch happens before validation, and none of them has a hook that runs after validation. BoringSSL already ships trust_anchors, which is a per-CertificateEntry extension from draft-ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids, and it sets client state on receipt at ssl/tls13_both.cc:325, in a state machine step earlier than ssl_verify_peer_cert.

This is not a claim that anything is broken today. Nothing implements this draft yet. It is why I think the deferral should be normative, rather than something each implementer has to work out again. In NSS in particular, deferring correctly is a two-part change that is not obvious: you stash the value in ss->xtnData, act after ssl3_AuthCertificate, and handle authCertificatePending separately.

Filed by Nazmus Salehin Sammo, Melbourne Institute of Technology, Melbourne, Australia. Student ID MIT252100. Contact: MIT252100@stud.mit.edu.au

issues.title: Section 3.4 port scoping vs Section 3.7 server obligation: client enforcement is narrower than the commitment
issues.author: Salehin-Sammo
issues.body:
This is a question about scope. I want to start by quoting Reddy's own review back, because I think it settles the principle, and it looks to me like it simply was not carried through to the port.

The argument already made, about ALPN
In PR #20 (2026-04-30), reviewing a proposal to include ALPN in the cache key:

The commitment is made by the server identity, not by the application protocol. A server that commits to PQC is committing at the server level, not per-ALPN. So including ALPN in the cache key would actually weaken the protection, a client connecting with a different ALPN would not benefit from the cached commitment and would be unprotected.

Yaron agreed, saying "You are right about ALPN ... Removing that text", and commit 8f600da removed it the same day.

I think that argument applies word for word to the port. A server that commits to PQC is committing at the server level, not per port. A client connecting on a different port would not benefit from the cached commitment and would be unprotected.

Why the port looks like the same case
The guarantee is stated at the level of the server. Section 1:

Clients reconnecting to an already known server within the validity period are protected from rollback to classical certificates.

The server's own obligation in Section 3.7, to use a PQC certificate "for that entire duration", carries no port qualifier. But Section 3.4 (L307-310) makes the client enforce at a narrower scope:

The client MUST key each cache entry by the authenticated TLS server identity from [RFC9525], the port, and whether the handshake is connection-oriented (TLS) or datagram (DTLS). Entries that differ in any of these MUST NOT be merged.

So the client enforces something narrower than the server has committed to. Someone who can steer one connection to a different port of the same authenticated identity reaches a cache miss and an unenforced handshake, while a valid commitment for that identity sits unexpired in the client's store. A forged HTTPS RR carrying a port SvcParam is enough, and per RFC 9460 Section 9.1 that does not change the origin.

What I am not claiming
This is not a bypass of a commitment that is in force. Under Section 3.4 no commitment is in force for the key that gets used. The mechanism does exactly what it says. I want to be clear about that, because it would be easy to overstate.

But I do not think it is the trust-on-first-use limitation that Section 5.1 documents either. A trust-on-first-use window is temporary. It happens once, and it closes as soon as the client makes an honest connection. Section 5.1's stated reason for accepting that limitation depends on exactly that self-healing behaviour:

if cache population is suppressed, the client would realize that the server is PQC-capable as soon as it connects directly to the server

That does not hold per port. The client will never connect honestly to those other ports, so those windows never close.

The HSTS comparison
Section 1 and Section 3.7 name HSTS as the model, and HSTS deliberately went the other way. It matches on the host component alone (RFC 6797 Section 8.3 step 1). It states that the policy "applies to HTTP over any TCP port of an HSTS Host" (Section 8.3). It makes that non-negotiable, saying "Hosts are unable to affect this aspect of HSTS Policy" (Appendix B). And it grounds the choice in the published argument against finer-grained origins (Section 2.1).

Every other part of the chain is also port-blind: the RFC 9525 reference identity, the certificate itself, and the cookie jar (RFC 6265 Section 8.5). The commitment appears to be the only port-scoped element.

I also note the direction of travel. The text originally keyed entries to the server identity alone. The port was added in commit 27ca7a1 (2026-04-17). Issue #13 is the only place I can find where the key is discussed, and it gives a DTLS disambiguation reason for the transport component and no reason at all for the port.

Separately, I have filed a question about which port Section 3.4 means, the authority port or the connected port (see #26 ). Which of those you intend decides whether the path described above is reachable.

Related but different
At IETF-126 (TLS session A, Meetecho chat log, 2026-07-23) Martin Thomson raised concerns about this cache key, saying it "won't work for browsers" and that "This sort of thing fails in multi-CDN deployments where the transition to PQ might not be uniform across the scope that the cache key identifies". That is a different concern from mine and it does not mention the port. I mention it only to make clear that I am not re-raising it.

The questions
Section 3.4 requires the cache key to include the port. Section 3.7 requires the server to present a PQC certificate "for that entire duration", with no port qualifier. Is the client meant to enforce a narrower scope than the server has committed to? Was the difference from HSTS intended? If it was, should Section 5 state the downgrade consequence?
Should host scoping be required for clients whose identities come from URIs, with port scoping kept only where a deployment really does run independent services on different ports?
Filed by Nazmus Salehin Sammo, Melbourne Institute of Technology, Melbourne, Australia. Student ID MIT252100. Contact: MIT252100@stud.mit.edu.au

issues.title: Resumed (PSK) handshakes carry no Certificate message, so Section 3.2's per-CertificateEntry MUST is vacuous
issues.author: Salehin-Sammo
issues.body:
The draft does not say anything about session resumption, and I think it needs to. All of the
enforcement is anchored on a message that a resumed handshake does not carry. RFC 8672 Section 2
handled this explicitly for the earlier mechanism, so there is a ready precedent to follow.

### The gap

Enforcement in Section 3.2 (L242-250) is stated over the `Certificate` message:

> ... the client MUST apply its PQC policy to **every CertificateEntry in the server's Certificate
> message** using the same criterion as in Section 3.1. If any CertificateEntry does not satisfy this
> requirement, the client MUST abort the handshake with a certificate_unknown alert.

RFC 8446 Section 4.4.2 says:

> The server MUST send a Certificate message whenever the agreed-upon key exchange method uses
> certificates for authentication (this includes all key exchange methods defined in this document
> **except PSK**).

and Section 2.2 describes the resumption flow directly:

> As the server is authenticating via a PSK, it does not send a Certificate or a CertificateVerify
> message.

So on a resumed handshake the trigger fires, because the client holds an unexpired commitment, but the
obligation applies to an empty set. The MUST is satisfied with nothing to check, and the MUST-abort
cannot fire. A conformant client has no normative basis to abort. It simply continues.

The same is true of the other enforcement points:

* Section 3.5 (L328-329) states the consequence: "As a result, the handshake would fail if a rollback
  attack is attempted." But `signature_algorithms` governs `CertificateVerify` (RFC 8446
  Section 4.2.3), and a resumed handshake has none, so this consequence does not hold in PSK mode.
* All three branches of Section 3.6 depend on receiving, or not receiving, the extension in the
  `Certificate` message. So none of them runs.

The draft contains no occurrence of `resumption`, `PSK`, `pre_shared_key`, `NewSessionTicket`,
`ticket`, `0-RTT` or `early data`.

### Visible independently in a second stack

Go's `crypto/tls` makes the same structure explicit in source. `readServerCertificate`
(`handshake_client_tls13.go:595-606`) returns before reading any `Certificate` message when a PSK is
in use:

```go
// Either a PSK or a certificate is always used, but not both.
// See RFC 8446, Section 4.1.1.
if hs.usingPSK {
    // Make sure the connection is still being verified whether or not this
    // is a resumption. Resumptions currently don't reverify certificates so
    // they don't call verifyServerCertificate. See Issue 31641.
    ...
    return nil
}
```

Any check an implementer attaches to the `Certificate` message is simply never reached on that path.

### Confirmed on a real stack

OpenSSL 3.6.2 with a genuine ML-DSA-65 chain, where the CA signature, the end-entity signature and the
end-entity subject public key are all ML-DSA-65:

| | Full handshake | Resumed (PSK) |
|---|---|---|
| session status | `New, TLSv1.3` | **`Reused, TLSv1.3`** |
| `Certificate` messages | 1 | **0** |
| `CertificateVerify` messages | 1 | **0** |
| `Finished` messages | 2 | 2 |

The resumed handshake completed successfully while carrying zero `Certificate` and zero
`CertificateVerify` messages. So this is a property of the specification, not of any attacker. A client
holding an unexpired PQ commitment can complete a session whose underlying authentication was
classical, and never consult the commitment. A PQ handshake does still issue resumable tickets, so this
is not moot for PQ deployments. A server running with tickets disabled is unaffected, but ticket
issuance is on by default.

### Why the RFC 8672 reasoning does not carry over unchanged

RFC 8672 Section 2 (Sheffer and Migault), covering the same TLS-layer pinning pattern:

> With TLS 1.3, session resumption is based on a Pre-Shared Key (PSK). This is orthogonal to this
> protocol. ... However, the protocol described in this document addresses the problem of misissued
> certificates. Thus, it is not expected to be used outside a certificate-based TLS key exchange, such
> as in PSK. **As a result, PSK handshakes MUST NOT include the extension defined here.**

The "orthogonal" conclusion rested on the threat model. Against misissuance, an attacker holding a
bogus certificate still cannot get a PSK without completing a handshake. Against the attacker this
draft names in Section 1, one holding an undisclosed CRQC, that no longer holds. Such an attacker can
break the ECDHE of a session it observes and derive the resumption PSK. The threat model changed, and
the exemption did not follow it into this draft.

### Bounding the impact honestly

I want to be careful not to overstate this, so I will state the limits myself.

* This is not a harvest-now, decrypt-later attack. RFC 8446 Section 4.6.1 caps ticket lifetime:
  "Servers MUST NOT use any value greater than 604800 seconds (7 days) ... Clients MUST NOT cache
  tickets for longer than 7 days, regardless of the ticket_lifetime". A CRQC that arrives years after a
  recording is useless against that ticket, because the client discarded the PSK long before. The
  attacker has to already hold a CRQC and act inside the ticket window. That is still exactly the
  attacker in Section 1, described there as one where "a CRQC may remain undisclosed, allowing
  attackers to exploit classical algorithms secretly". But it is a narrower window than a recording
  attack.
* It is not indefinitely extensible. Tickets minted by an impersonating attacker are that attacker's
  own, so extending requires continuous presence, not a single break.
* The mechanism is not new. RFC 8446 Section 4.6.1 flags the general hazard, that resumption chains can
  "indefinitely extend the lifetime of the keying material originally derived from an initial non-PSK
  handshake (which was most likely tied to the peer's certificate)", and it recommends limits on total
  keying-material lifetime. My point is only that this draft neither cites that nor says anything about
  resumption.

Even setting the attacker aside completely, the specification gap stands on its own. A document that
states a lasting cross-connection guarantee should say what happens in the handshake mode where its
enforcement points do not exist.

### Possible fixes, least invasive first

1. **Security Considerations only.** Add a subsection saying that resumption skips enforcement because
   there is no `Certificate` message, as RFC 8672 Section 2 did. This closes the silence with no
   normative change.
2. **Follow the RFC 8672 precedent, normatively.** State that a client holding an unexpired commitment
   MUST NOT resume via PSK to that server, unless the PSK comes from a handshake that itself satisfied
   the commitment. In other words, tie enforcement to the handshake the ticket came from.
3. **Stronger.** Also require clients to record the credential class of the handshake that established
   each PSK, refuse resumption where that class is classical while a commitment is in force, and bound
   total keying-material lifetime per RFC 8446 Section 4.6.1.

Option 1 on its own would be a real improvement. I have no strong view between 2 and 3.

### Supporting model, optional reading

I have a Tamarin model of PSK provenance, which records the credential class of the handshake that
established each ticket. It falsifies commitment binding when resumption is unguarded, and verifies it
when a committed client resumes only PSKs of PQ origin. It is a model of the Section 3.2 and
Section 3.6 client state machine, not a security proof of TLS 1.3. The OpenSSL result above is the
stronger evidence. I am happy to share either.

### Context

I am an MRes student doing formal analysis of the PQ authentication negotiation drafts. I have read
`-02` in full, along with the tracker (all issues, `state=all`) and the list threads. This is separate
from issue #23.

Filed by Nazmus Salehin Sammo, Melbourne Institute of Technology, Melbourne, Australia.

pulls.title: Technical consistency improvements
pulls.author: yaronf
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR addresses technical consistency issues identified in the draft:

- **Bidirectional scope clarification**: Abstract and introduction now explicitly state the mechanism works peer-to-peer, with typical use being client-caching-server but also supporting server-caching-client
- **Cache update logic**: Clarified that when switching algorithms, use the new validity period from the extension
- **Zero value semantics**: Defined that `algorithm_validity_period` of zero means don't cache (if no cache exists) or clear cache (if exists)
- **Validation requirements**: Specified that `signature_algorithm` must match certificate and must be a PQC algorithm
- **Extension presence logic**: Clarified that when using traditional (non-PQC) certificate, sender should send extension with no data to indicate support
- **Commitment timing**: Clarified that duration is measured from the current TLS handshake

## Changes

All changes improve clarity and consistency without changing the fundamental protocol design.

reviews.author: tireddy2
reviews.body: Most of the changes look good to me.

comments.body: The commitment is made by the server identity, not by the application protocol. A server that commits to PQC is committing at the server level, not per-ALPN. So including ALPN in the cache key would actually weaken the protection, a client connecting with a different ALPN would not benefit from the cached commitment and would be unprotected.
Thanks. You are right about ALPN (which could be used in theory for cert selection but apparently this would not be a good idea). Removing that text.

pulls.title: Threat model, deployment, and Security Considerations (PR 2)
pulls.author: yaronf
pulls.body:
Implements the PR-2 batch from the issue plan:

- **#5** — Introduction: CRQC / rollback threat narrative; informative {{RescorlaPQEmergency}} reference.
- **#6** — {{certificate-chain}}: reject mixed chains when PQC is required (`certificate_unknown`).
- **#7** — Operational: CDNs / changing chains; TLS-terminating intermediaries and RFC 7469 carve-out analogy.
- **#18** — Security Considerations: first-connection trust, cache-churn DoS mitigations.

@tireddy2, requesting your review when you have a chance.

Made with [Cursor](https://cursor.com)

comments.body:
I propose modifying the last line as follows:
For a fully PQ-signed path through the PKI, trust anchors would also need to be PQ-capable where they participate in validation; this document does not specify trust-store policy.
I think specifying chain validation policy is out of scope for this draft. I propose to retain only the first paragraph and drop the second paragraph.
I would say: Traditional  certificate chains remain out of scope except where this document already requires rejection (see {{certificate-chain}}).

A malicious server can only affect clients that are already successfully completing handshakes with it, meaning the client already trusts it. The more realistic concern is a mis-configured server rather than a malicious one.
""meaningfully change" is vague.
I suggest removing this paragraph, TLS WG does not like middleboxes :(

I disagree. This mechanism would not achieve its goal if a mixed chain is being used. So we're not saying that mixed chains are forbidden. What we're saying is, you cannot have a mixed chain along with PQC Continuity.

The first paragraph is basically rationale for the normative text in the second one.
You're right, but there's actual normative text here and it's important in practice. Would it be better if we moved it to an appendix?
You're probably right that this is a theoretical concern. I don't think any kind of misconfiguration can cause it - you need an actively malicious server for this attack.
Yes, moving to Appendix works for me.
If it is a malicious server, it could cause a lot more damage to the client :)

The first paragraph says "many deployments will continue to rely on classical roots" which may be true currently  but could be cited for years as justification for not migrating the full chain, which undermines the entire purpose of the draft.  I suggest to simplify the text and say something like:
Post-quantum authentication requires signatures along the entire path to be resistant to quantum-capable adversaries; a PQC end-entity certificate paired with a classically signed intermediate does not provide this property.

Thought about it some more, I'd rather keep it as-is, because:

- There's a bit of normative text, which doesn't read well in an appendix.
- Right now it's under "operational considerations", so not the core protocol.
Absolutely. But does that justify removing this section completely?
